Peter Pathappan The Phonetic Value of Gardiner’s Sign U 23 (𓍋) in Earlier Egyptian The article examines the reading of the sign 𓍋 in the Old and Middle Kingdom and concludes that the phonetic value must be mr and not mḥr. Four pieces of evidence are used to support this conclusion. The first three come from onomastics and show the interchangeability of 𓍋 with 𓅓𓂋, 𓈘, and 𓌸. The fourth piece of evidence is a prefixed form of the verb 𓍋𓅓𓂋𓅪 from the Pyramid Texts, which proves that the verb consists of two radicals, meaning that it must be mr and not mḥr. T he sign 𓍋 possesses two distinct phonetic values. While the reading ꜣb is not subject to debate, the second phonetic value has been the subject of scientific discourse for some time. The prevailing perspective, as articulated by Gardiner (1957: 518), is that the phonetic value is mr. Quack (2003) posited that an alternative reading, mḥr, should be employed. He cites late spellings with ḥ and a pun from the Pyramid Texts. This assertion is countered by the works of Regulski (2010: 196) and Schweitzer (2011). Evidence from the Early Dynastic Period is cited, and it is asserted that this evidence can only be explained by the phonetic value mr. This question has been addressed in another article by Quack (2022). In addition, he presents a series of arguments that are intended to support his hypothesis. He also endeavors to invalidate the evidence cited by Regulski and Schweitzer. A thorough review of this article was conducted by Fante (2023). She has demonstrated with a high degree of

She has demonstrated with a high degree of conviction that the evidence from the Early Dynastic Period unequivocally validates the phonetic value mr. Moreover, she has substantiated that Quack's interpretations of the Early Dynastic Period evidence are not valid, and that all the evidence from the Old and Middle Kingdom that Quack lists for mḥr, including the attempt of Collombert (2010) equating the different terms for “pyramid” 𓍋𓅓𓂋𓉴 and 𓁷𓂋𓉴,1 is untenable. Additionally, she proposes an explanatory model for the late spellings with ḥ. The sign has undergone a process of reinterpretation, a phenomenon that has also been observed in 𓋉 or 𓏤𓏤𓏤𓏤𓏤𓏤𓏤𓏤.2 This finding serves to substantiate the phonetic value of mr as valid for the duration of the Early Dynastic Period. David Mihalyfy Urbana, Illinois, USA Explaining the Odd Foot Sign of Gardiner D58 in the Egyptian Negator Transliterated bn: A Case for Innovative Orthographic Reuse Based on the Phonetic Reduction of the Nominalizer bw (> -ⲞⲨ-) and the Non-Etymological Writing bw nb for wn nb (> ⲞⲨⲞⲚ ⲚⲒⲘ) In the mid-2nd millennium BCE, Egyptian scribes began writing a common negator as bn, with an odd foot sign of Gardiner D58 at its start. Building on past scholarship that recognizes the sign’s semantic function and a larger, pre-existing orthographic link between negation and other body parts, this analysis identifies why disambiguation was needed in this specific case and why this specific sign was chosen as a disambiguator. On the one hand, the negator was at risk of confusion for other sentence-beginning entities potentially representable as a bare n. On the other hand, the not infrequent nominalizer bw that was also used to spell the word bw nb “everyone” began with a phonetically reduced b

I n the mid-2nd millennium BCE, Egyptian scribes began writing a common negator as bn, “[f]or reasons that are still unclear…” 1 The crux of the mystery is the odd foot sign of Gardiner D58 that is transliterated b. Aptly called “a semantic indicator of negation,” it has also been identified as participating in a larger, pre-existing orthographic link between negation and other body parts, namely the open arms sign of Gardiner D35 that begins the sequence transliterated as nn.2 However, this very plausible general influence does not explain why a semantic indicator of negation might have been needed with this specific negator, nor does it explain the specific choice of this foot sign of Gardiner D58 versus some other body part hieroglyph. Perhaps a bit surprisingly for ancillary questions about the function of a single monoconsonantal hieroglyph, the path towards progress on both fronts primarily lies in underappreciated and unacknowledged evidence found in Coptic. Previous conceptualizations of the mentioned phenomena are surprisingly questionable when a larger range of comparanda are introduced. Effectively, previous conceptualizations posit two different diachronic replacements across Egyptian’s history. First, previous conceptualizations imply that the same root first figured into one kind of adverbial phrase and then into another, later, and purportedly unrelated kind of adverbial phrase – namely, m bw mꜣꜥ “truly/truthfully” as seen in the newlyadduced parallels, and then the purported indefinite article-incorporating construction seen in Ϩ︦ⲚⲞⲨⲘⲈ “truly” (< ẖnw wꜥ mꜣꜥ). Second, previous conceptualizations also imply that the word “everyone” also first took one major form and then another, later, and purportedly unrelated form – namely, bw nb “everyone,” and then the ⲞⲨⲞⲚ ⲚⲒⲘ “everyone” of Coptic. Aufrère CNRS, Aix-Marseille Université, TDMAM, Aix-en-Provence, France Académie des Sciences et Lettres de Montpellier Le prisme typhonien : faune, flore, minéraux et passions nuisibles d’après Plutarque (Isis et Osiris, 50) Cette étude démontre que dans la pensée sacerdotale égyptienne considérée sous le prisme étique par Plutarque, le dieu Typhon-Seth fusionne en un continuum absolu le désordre de la nature et la déchéance morale. Le philosophe synthétise cette vision en la déployant en trois volets qui lient les animaux venimeux, dangereux ou stupides, les végétaux toxiques et les passions humaines néfastes (vices), tous définis comme des objets d’emprise directe du dieu. Du point de vue émique des théologiens, cette pensée postule qu’un crime moral ou une déviance sexuelle relèvent d’une perturbation d’essence cosmique de même ordre. La fureur, la cruauté ou la stérilité (qui justifie l’interdiction des eunuques à l’Abaton de Philae) découleraient de la même force brute

. La fureur, la cruauté ou la stérilité (qui justifie l’interdiction des eunuques à l’Abaton de Philae) découleraient de la même force brute séthienne qui dessèche les sycomores sacrés, tarit les sources, libère le venin des serpents, fait surgir le sel de la mer ou le salpêtre de la terre, se traduit par la médiocrité des qualités des simples. L’étude, en déconstruisant de façon sur-étique le regard étique de Plutarque, restitue un système interconnecté où les vices de l’homme et les désordres causés par des hôtes de l’environnement sont les manifestations indissociables d’une seule et même essence chaotique. Toutefois, l’analyse de Plutarque témoigne d’un réductionnisme étique qui, loin de traduire la richesse théologique du dieu Seth, finit par fossiliser une sur-systématisation d’époque romaine employée à des fins politiques et morales, laquelle permet de déshumaniser Cléopâtre en l’associant à de déplaisants monstres du Nil. L’éthologie animale comme miroir des vices humains Pour les Égyptiens, les silhouettes des animaux typhoniens ne sont pas seulement des dangers physiques, elles essentialisent des déviances psychologiques et comportementales qui émergent dans les nuages sémantiques attachés aux épithètes qu’on leur donne et aux mots qu’ils déterminent. L’éthologie propre des trois espèces séthiennes majeures fournit un répertoire de métaphores morales immédiatement déchiffrables par la société nilotique. L’âne sauvage (onagre) incarne la colère aveugle, la fureur irraisonnée, la lubricité et l’obstination. Le crocodile et l’hippopotame matérialisent la voracité, la rapacité, la cruauté gratuite et le meurtre par embuscade.

F rom antiquity to the present day, ancient Egypt has always drawn attention and sparked the interest of people all around the world. There were, of course, moments of greater importance, such as the period following Napoleon’s expedition to Egypt (1798–1801) and the period following the discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb (1922). This led to the most diverse expressions of recuperation, reception, reinvention, and recreation of the Egyptian past. From architecture to furniture, from cinema to video games, from literature to comics, for years (even centuries) ancient Egypt was a constant presence through the adoption and adaptation of its themes, symbolism, and even its fantastical imaginary. Historical Background – The Development of Egyptomania in the 19th Century/Beginning of the 20th Century The interest in ancient Egyptian civilisation, whether for its culture, religion, and mythology, or for its art and symbolism, did not arise after Napoleon’s expedition to Egypt (1798–1801). Even earlier, as far back as the classical civilisations, ancient Egypt was a matter of interest and was the subject of many different uses and reuses (Bednarski, 2010; Lloyd, 2010). However, it is after the expedition that we see the most varied adaptations of Egyptian themes emerge in a resounding fashion in a great number of aesthetic manifestations, such as architecture, furniture, different types of artefacts, interior design, and performing arts (Curl, 2005, 225), but also in fashion, mainly in jewellery (Nadelhoffer, 2007, 144–149; Geczy, 2013, 80; Parramore, 2008, 22–4). The expedition to Egypt, the first great imperialistic incursion into the Near East of modern times, is one of the most remarkable events of the transition from the 18th century to the 19th century, with huge repercussions on the political, military, and cultural scene. It is a milestone with lasting consequences in the scientific rediscovery of the ancient pharaonic civilisation (Bret, 1996, 215). This was a ‘strange endeavour’. Plans for the endeavour began in 1797, when the French Directory, weakened by the previous wars and strongly marked by the economic struggles and popular uprisings, decided, on the 5th of March 1798, to send to Egypt one of the best armies of the Republic under the command of its most brilliant general, dressed in wool uniforms for a hot climate, without declaring war or even letting the troops know where they were headed (Laurens, 1997, 29–40). And, on the 19th of May 1798, under the command of General Napoleon Bonaparte, a powerful army and a huge fleet of ships left Toulon and headed to an unknown destination, towards an adventure that would last until 1801. By Napoleon’s order, alongside the soldiers, the expedition was composed of a number of engineers, architects, naturalists, botanists, geographers, mineralogists, antiquarians, orientalists, painters, draughtsmen, engravers, and writers, with their characteristic study and working tools (Vercoutter, 1986, 39–55; Sales, 2007, 16; Laurens, 1997, 46, 47). This was the first time that a scientific delegation, by political invitation, joined a military campaign. Between 1798 and 1801, amid a series of massacres, riots, victories, and losses that threatened the French political, military, and economic success, Napoleon Bonaparte’s expedition opened a different era in relations between East and West concerning culture and science. These events, spanning the 19th and early 20th centuries, stimulated interest in and the resulting (re)use of ancient Egyptian themes. Before ending this review, we should mention other developments that were both responses to these and other stimuli— such as new archaeological discoveries10 or exhibitions of Egyptian art—and new triggers of Egyptomania themselves. We’re talking, for example, about the growth of Egypt as a tourist destination (Fritze, 2016, 187–8; Humbert, 1989, 30), but also about its growing presence in art, cinema,11 opera, ballet, literature, and advertising (Fazzini and McKercher, 2001, 463; Humbert, 2015, 472–78).

Considering the period between Napoleon’s expedition and the discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb, there were many archaeological discoveries in Egypt. Until 1850, the discoveries were due to a mixture of adventurers, diplomats, and proto-archaeologists, of whom we can highlight Giovanni Belzoni, who, between 1816 and 1818, worked in Abu Simbel, on the tomb of Seti I, on the pyramid of Khafre, etc., being responsible for the transfer of many artefacts to the British Museum; from 1850 onwards, we have the first archaeologists: Mariette (for example: 1851 – Serapeum of Sakkara; 1857 – tombs of the Thebes region, where he recovered many pieces of jewellery); and Anthony Charles Harris (1855 – Rhind Tomb). During the “golden years”, between 1881 and 1914, there were many discoveries, such as the one by Maspero (1881 – royal mummies in the cachette of Deir el-Bahari), by Petrie (1888 – portraits of the Fayum, the tombs in Bubastis and in the Valley of Kings; 1891–2 – Akhenaton’s Palaces, in Tell el-Amarna), by Theodore Davis (1902–14 – multiple discoveries in the Valley of Kings), and by Ernesto Schiaparelli (1904 – Nefertari’s tomb, in the Valley of Queens).

To end the analysis of ancient Egypt’s influence in fashion between Napoleon’s expedition to Egypt and the discovery of Pharaoh Tutankhamun’s tomb, we should still mention the colours. The contact with the iconography of ancient Egypt did not solely influence the shapes and motifs of clothing; it also had a strong impact on colours. The colours of the tomb’s walls (Fig. 16), of the artefacts, and of Egypt itself inspired a wide range of fabric colours used in clothing, hats, and accessories. Conclusion “Dame Fashion is protesting loudly that, wherever her genius rules this season, the Egyptian motif and silhouette are to be accorded a place of honor.” (Harper’s – May 1920) In fashion, as in most domains of Western culture, the growing familiarity with ancient Egypt resulting from Napoleon’s expedition to Egypt and all the events that followed – from monumental publications, to the great Exhibitions, to an increasing number of archaeological excavations – meant the adoption and adaptation of a multitude of influences from this civilisation. The discovery of Pharaoh Tutankhamun’s tomb on the 4th of November 1922 and the resulting wave of Tutmania that spread worldwide are usually taken as the main milestone in the development and the peak of interest in ancient Egypt. Truthfully, the whole period considered in this text, specifically the 19th century and the first decades of the 20th century (including 1922), gives us many examples of appropriation of ancient Egypt in fashion. Women’s and fashion magazines, mainly European but also American, show, throughout the studied period, an increasing interest in importing drawings, inspirations, clothing styles and even colours from ancient Egypt. In 1801, we identify the first reference to a colour of Egyptian inspiration; in 1812, the first Egyptian robe; in 1835, there is the Egyptian pattern; and in 1848, we have the mantelet cleopatra. But the analysis also makes it very clear that it is in the early years of the 20th century that ancient Egypt assumes a prominent position in women’s clothing and accessories. Thus, whether through the use of overt Egyptian symbols – scarabs, sphinx, hieroglyphs, etc. – through the attribution of Egyptian inspiration to sometimes undefined patterns (Egyptian pattern), or through references to clothing styles (Egyptian style), the truth is that the more familiar Egyptian civilisation became to the public, the more it was used as an inspiration for European and American fashion. Thus, when, at the end of 1922, Tutankhamun appeared in newspapers and became a world-famous figure, Egypt’s influence in fashion had already undergone a period of growth, with a more and more evident and diversified presence.
